samples.text:
The graph shows the electricity demand in a city during a normal day in winter and a normal day in summer, in gigawatts.

In winter, the demand at midnight was 32 gigawatts and it went down to 28 at 03:00, which is the lowest. Then it increased to 42 at 09:00. Between 09:00 and 15:00 it was nearly the same, about 40. After that, it reached the peak of 47 gigawatts at 18:00 and then it fall to 33 at the end of the day.

In summer, the demand was lower in the night. It was 22 at midnight and 19 at 03:00. From 06:00 it went up quick and in 15:00 it was 43, the highest point for summer. This was the only time when summer was more than winter. After this, the demand decreased to 39 at 18:00 and 23 at the end.

Overall, winter demand was higher than summer in most of the day. The winter peak was in the evening but the summer peak was in the afternoon.
samples.why: Overview at the end but identifies the key contrast · main features described chronologically in a mechanical way · adequate vocabulary · adverb, preposition and tense errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The line graph compares the amount of electricity used in a city over a 24-hour period on a typical winter day and a typical summer day.

Overall, demand was higher in winter for most of the day. Both seasons followed a similar pattern, with the lowest use in the early morning, but they peaked at different times: in the early evening in winter and in the mid-afternoon in summer.

On the winter day, demand stood at 32 gigawatts at midnight and dipped to its lowest point of 28 gigawatts at 03:00. It then rose sharply to 42 gigawatts by 09:00 and remained around 40 gigawatts until 15:00. The highest demand of the day, 47 gigawatts, was recorded at 18:00, after which consumption declined to 33 gigawatts by midnight.

The summer day showed lower figures overall, starting at 22 gigawatts and falling to 19 gigawatts at 03:00. However, demand grew steadily from 06:00 onwards, reaching a peak of 43 gigawatts at 15:00. This was the only point at which summer consumption exceeded that of winter. Following this, it fell back gradually and finished the day on 23 gigawatts.
samples.why: Clear overview identifying different peak times · logical progression by season · good range of cohesive devices and vocabulary · frequent error-free sentences with only minor imprecision.

samples.text:
The graph illustrates fluctuations in a city's electricity demand, measured in gigawatts, across a typical winter day and a typical summer day.

In general, winter demand was higher than summer demand for almost the entire day. While both followed a broadly similar daily cycle, with a trough in the early hours, the timing of their peaks differed: winter consumption was greatest in the early evening, whereas summer consumption peaked in the afternoon.

In winter, demand began at 32 gigawatts at midnight and fell to a low of 28 gigawatts at 03:00. It then climbed steeply during the morning to 42 gigawatts at 09:00 and held relatively steady at around 40 gigawatts until mid-afternoon. A sharp evening surge followed, taking demand to a daily high of 47 gigawatts at 18:00, before it eased back to 33 gigawatts by the end of the day.

Summer demand was consistently lower overnight, bottoming out at 19 gigawatts at 03:00, some nine gigawatts below the winter figure. From 06:00, however, it rose continuously to reach 43 gigawatts at 15:00, briefly overtaking winter demand. It then declined steadily through the evening, returning to 23 gigawatts at midnight.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected, especially the differing peak times and single crossover · clear overview · accurate figures and comparison · precise vocabulary such as 'trough' and 'bottoming out' · error-free, varied structures.
